articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India needs to create an entire ecosystem for recycling of lithium-ion batteries

On November 10, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade banned the export of lithium-ion battery black mass by moving it from the “free” to the “prohibited” list of exports. Black mass is an intermediate product when spent batteries and factory scrap are shredded. It contains valuable lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and graphite. The Commerce Ministry says the ban will ensure feedstock for domestic refiners, lift their capacity utilisation and draw investment. While the recycling of lead-acid batteries end-to-end is an established ecosystem and formalised, too, lithium-ion battery recycling is an emerging segment with only a few dozen licensed operators but has much potential given the scale of use of such batteries in EVs. While the ban will redirect supply, it will not automatically create a market and ecosystem. Just banning export without creating an entire ecosystem will only lead to dumping of lithium-ion batteries into landfills if the blackmass has no market. Blackmass production is a largely mechanical process but further downstream processing is more specialised chemical processing requiring larger investment and further policy support. If downstream units are online, their output can directly feed into indigenous lithium-ion battery manufacture.

India depends heavily on imports for critical minerals such as those used in battery inputs. Beyond working on supply aspects, the government must address the price gap to create a robust recycling market. Under the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, producers buy extended producer responsibility (EPR) certificates from recyclers but these are undervalued. Cheap certificates reward recycling on paper over investment in high-yield plants. A floor price that covers the full cost of recovery, with digital tracking, would fix that. Rare earths show how recycling remains a missed opportunity for India because of policy gaps. A smartphone can be up to 1% neodymium-iron-boron magnet by weight. That puts its rare earth content at about 3,000 parts per million, comparable to India’s monazite beach sands. Extracting it takes less energy than mining. A magnet separated from the phone is about 30% rare earth. Magnets make up as much as 3% of a hard drive, but are usable only if they are removed before the drive is shredded for data destruction. Yet the e-waste rules do not require rare earth separation. Rare earths need a separate EPR category, too. Payment by weight cannot be applied for rare earth minerals.

articles.title: In a dilemma: On Sheikh Hasina and India-Bangladesh ties
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India must improve ties with Bangladesh, and protect Hasina

Bangladesh’s former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina now in exile in India, has set off speculation about her imminent return to Dhaka by submitting an application for a new Bangladeshi passport and national identity card this week. The application, made through the Bangladesh High Commission in Delhi, was dismissed by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s Foreign Affairs Adviser Humayun Kabir, who said that the government in Dhaka would not grant a passport to a “terrorist”, and would seek her return via the extradition agreement as a “prisoner transfer process” with India. Ms. Hasina has already announced that she plans to return to Bangladesh in December this year, as she did after her previous stay in India in exile from 1975-1981, after the brutal assassination of her father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and nearly every other member of her family. However, the situation is considerably different now. This time, Ms. Hasina came to India in 2024 fleeing mobs of protestors that overthrew her government, and has since been convicted by a tribunal for ordering a crackdown on thousands of students, and sentenced to death. In interviews, including to The Hindu , Ms. Hasina says she hopes to return to Bangladesh to argue her case and rebuild her party, the Awami League, but that is hardly likely, given the anger against her amongst the polity, and bipartisan consensus to ban the Awami League from politics. Despite the harsh rhetoric it employs against her, the BNP government is unlikely to wish for her return, as it would have to begin execution proceedings against the 79-year-old former Prime Minister, with international opposition to such a move expected to be voluble. Not doing so would only strengthen its opposition party, the Jamaat-e-Islami, that has accused the Rahman government of soft-pedalling the issue. The government must also worry about possible protests and violence within the country in the event Ms. Hasina returns.

The situation puts the Modi government in a spot. Ever since Ms. Hasina announced plans to return, during a virtual press conference held in Delhi on August 5 this year, Delhi-Dhaka ties have been on a downslide. The government’s decision not to prevent Ms. Hasina from addressing the press, where she used the opportunity to soundly criticise PM Rahman, meant the abrupt cancellation of the Bangladesh PM’s visit. Next month, the Indo-Bangladesh Ganga Water treaty is set to expire, and talks on its extension have also become a casualty. Ms. Hasina has been an honoured guest in India, and the government cannot physically restrain her from taking the flight to Dhaka or travelling to the land border at Petrapole to cross over. Nor can it wash its hands of her situation once she crosses over. New Delhi must redouble its diplomatic efforts on improving bilateral ties while also ensuring Ms. Hasina’s welfare.

Editorial Context: In a dilemma: On Sheikh Hasina and India-Bangladesh ties. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

articles.summary: India must improve ties with Bangladesh, and protect Hasina
articles.keyPoints:
• India must improve ties with Bangladesh, and protect Hasina
• Bangladesh’s former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina now in exile in India, has set off speculation about her imminent return to Dhaka by submitting an application for a new Bangladeshi passport and national identity card this week. The application, made through the Bangladesh High Commission in Delhi, was dismissed by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s Foreign Affairs Adviser Humayun Kabir, who said that the government in Dhaka would not grant a passport to a “terrorist”, and would seek her return via the extradition agreement as a “prisoner transfer process” with India. Ms. Hasina has already announced that she plans to return to Bangladesh in December this year, as she did after her previous stay in India in exile from 1975-1981, after the brutal assassination of her father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and nearly every other member of her family. However, the situation is considerably different now. This time, Ms. Hasina came to India in 2024 fleeing mobs of protestors that overthrew her government, and has since been convicted by a tribunal for ordering a crackdown on thousands of students, and sentenced to death. In interviews, including to The Hindu , Ms. Hasina says she hopes to return to Bangladesh to argue her case and rebuild her party, the Awami League, but that is hardly likely, given the anger against her amongst the polity, and bipartisan consensus to ban the Awami League from politics. Despite the harsh rhetoric it employs against her, the BNP government is unlikely to wish for her return, as it would have to begin execution proceedings against the 79-year-old former Prime Minister, with international opposition to such a move expected to be voluble. Not doing so would only strengthen its opposition party, the Jamaat-e-Islami, that has accused the Rahman government of soft-pedalling the issue. The government must also worry about possible protests and violence within the country in the event Ms. Hasina returns.
• The situation puts the Modi government in a spot. Ever since Ms. Hasina announced plans to return, during a virtual press conference held in Delhi on August 5 this year, Delhi-Dhaka ties have been on a downslide. The government’s decision not to prevent Ms. Hasina from addressing the press, where she used the opportunity to soundly criticise PM Rahman, meant the abrupt cancellation of the Bangladesh PM’s visit. Next month, the Indo-Bangladesh Ganga Water treaty is set to expire, and talks on its extension have also become a casualty. Ms. Hasina has been an honoured guest in India, and the government cannot physically restrain her from taking the flight to Dhaka or travelling to the land border at Petrapole to cross over. Nor can it wash its hands of her situation once she crosses over. New Delhi must redouble its diplomatic efforts on improving bilateral ties while also ensuring Ms. Hasina’s welfare.

fullParagraphs: Nations must deliver on past promises before committing to lofty climate goals

The 31st Conference of Parties (COP) began this week in Antalya, Türkiye. Hosted by Türkiye and negotiations presided over by Australia, the run-up to the gathering saw ministerial delegations visit Fiji and Tuvalu. This was to serve as a stark reminder of the purpose of COPs, namely that it was small island nations that are most vulnerable to warming from rising greenhouse gas emissions. However, the opening days have belied this sense of urgency. Prominent world leaders, even from the European countries who as a group champion the cause most vociferously, have chosen to skip the meet. The agenda and pre-summit expectations suggest that the main concerns this year are likely to be about delivering on existing commitments such as delivering $300 billion a year by 2035, which was decided at COP29 in Baku, as well as the COP30 call to triple the adaptation finance during that interval. However, deciding how these climate funds will practically flow has been deferred to COP32. The second global stocktake, a periodic check on progress under the Paris Agreement, begins at COP31, but the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has dithered on a timeline for the next reports that will serve as the scientific push to policy makers to accelerate efforts towards keeping a rise in temperatures below 2°C, and more ambitiously 1.5°C.

The previous edition of COP30 concluded without a formal roadmap away from fossil fuels — a step back from the COP28 consensus in Dubai. There is a voluntary roadmap ahead of COP31 but it is out of the formal negotiating text. In the background of the West Asia war, the withdrawal of the United States from the Paris Agreement and financial strain writ large over Europe, funds are a challenge as evidenced in the recent Loss and Damage fund approval to Nepal of $21 million when the ask is in billions. COP31 president, Murat Kurum has laid an electrification target, which is to raise electricity’s share from 23% of total energy consumption to 35% by 2035. India has already refused to sign such a pledge and insisted on predictable climate finance, technology transfer, and nationally determined approaches to climate mitigation. These negotiations have a character of their own and deliberating nations must strive to get nations to deliver on past promises rather than commit to new lofty targets.

articles.title: Visions of the future: On this year’s Booker Prize
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: This year’s Booker Prize betrays an anxiety about AI’s place in society

A defining feature of the world today is that knowledge is proliferating and societies are struggling to agree on what is happening. AI models have significantly catalysed this devolution, allowing bad actors to flood spaces ranging from the research literature to public airwaves with questionable information, and drawing the attention of governments worldwide to the security implications of such a potent technology. The Booker Prize for M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything , a novel about a sense-defying alien invasion and the unsettling prospect of un-understandability it confronts humans with, effectively acknowledges the centrality of the AI question both through the book’s substance and the judges’ choice. A consequence of rampant AI use has been an assault on people’s attention span as well as the ability to make sense of new claims, so much so that reliable, verifiable meaning has become a premium entity. The novel, on the other hand, attempts to diagnose a post-meaning world in which people are only left to look inward. The Prize is also a long-overdue victory for the merits of science fiction, a genre that Harrison helped shape from the late 1960s, and one that English literature’s top honours have repeatedly overlooked. That said, the novel itself is far from being its best example, including because Harrison’s diagnosis lets technology and the practice of power off the hook for their failures.

One of the judges said she had also sought a book “only a human being could write”, but defending a novel for its ability to thumb its nose at the machines is unfair to the literary enterprise and betrays a wider public anxiety about AI, especially over the lack of consensus about its proper place in society. OpenAI has been aggravating these deliberations among mathematicians by using its machines to make headway, in record time, on problems that have been unsolved for decades, without also contributing to mathematical education and research. Anthropic , the American company known for its Claude AI model, has announced its IPO with a surprising proposed valuation of $1.4 trillion . Since much of this is pegged on speculative future demand for AI services, the same absence of consensus leaves room for investors to imagine an enormous market for Anthropic’s products and invest to help the company realise them, thus narrowing the space for society to deliberate on all competing visions of the future. And while The End of Everything , with its philosophy of pragmatic absurdism, offers poor guidance on how to keep that space open, doing so ultimately remains one of the most important unfinished tasks before the world today.

articles.summary: This year’s Booker Prize betrays an anxiety about AI’s place in society
articles.keyPoints:
• This year’s Booker Prize betrays an anxiety about AI’s place in society
• A defining feature of the world today is that knowledge is proliferating and societies are struggling to agree on what is happening. AI models have significantly catalysed this devolution, allowing bad actors to flood spaces ranging from the research literature to public airwaves with questionable information, and drawing the attention of governments worldwide to the security implications of such a potent technology. The Booker Prize for M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything , a novel about a sense-defying alien invasion and the unsettling prospect of un-understandability it confronts humans with, effectively acknowledges the centrality of the AI question both through the book’s substance and the judges’ choice. A consequence of rampant AI use has been an assault on people’s attention span as well as the ability to make sense of new claims, so much so that reliable, verifiable meaning has become a premium entity. The novel, on the other hand, attempts to diagnose a post-meaning world in which people are only left to look inward. The Prize is also a long-overdue victory for the merits of science fiction, a genre that Harrison helped shape from the late 1960s, and one that English literature’s top honours have repeatedly overlooked. That said, the novel itself is far from being its best example, including because Harrison’s diagnosis lets technology and the practice of power off the hook for their failures.
• One of the judges said she had also sought a book “only a human being could write”, but defending a novel for its ability to thumb its nose at the machines is unfair to the literary enterprise and betrays a wider public anxiety about AI, especially over the lack of consensus about its proper place in society. OpenAI has been aggravating these deliberations among mathematicians by using its machines to make headway, in record time, on problems that have been unsolved for decades, without also contributing to mathematical education and research. Anthropic , the American company known for its Claude AI model, has announced its IPO with a surprising proposed valuation of $1.4 trillion . Since much of this is pegged on speculative future demand for AI services, the same absence of consensus leaves room for investors to imagine an enormous market for Anthropic’s products and invest to help the company realise them, thus narrowing the space for society to deliberate on all competing visions of the future. And while The End of Everything , with its philosophy of pragmatic absurdism, offers poor guidance on how to keep that space open, doing so ultimately remains one of the most important unfinished tasks before the world today.

articles.title: Milking power: On the overturning of Gokul Dairy cooperative mandate
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: The overturning of the mandate in the Gokul Dairy cooperative is disturbing

Amid a nationwide outcry over electoral malpractices, with fresh evidence emerging every day, the BJP government in Maharashtra has gone a step further in overturning a popular mandate through an executive fiat. It approved changing the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act through an ordinance on November 4 — which the Governor promulgated on November 6 — with the immediate effect of facilitating the takeover of the Kolhapur District Cooperative Milk Producers’ Union, popularly known as Gokul Dairy , by the BJP and its allies. A Congress-led panel won 13 of the 25 elected seats on the board of the cooperative on October 19. Gokul, which is one of Maharashtra’s most influential cooperative institutions, has an annual turnover of around ₹4,000 crore and is linked to several lakh milk producers in western Maharashtra. The BJP had set its eyes on the cooperative sector as yet another arena of its political dominance, creating a Ministry of Cooperation under Home Minister Amit Shah. While that plan of controlling cooperatives continues to play out through various means, the overturning of an election clearly won by the Congress-led Opposition marks a new level of brazenness by the BJP, and of the impunity its actions continue to receive from the judiciary.

The Congress-backed Rajarshi Shahu Shetkari Samvichari Aghadi, led by Satej Patil, won 13 of the 25 elected seats on the Gokul board. On October 29, the election of the chairman was deadlocked after the BJP-allied members did not participate, and the meeting fell short of the required quorum of 14 members. The directors allied to the Congress and its partners subsequently declared Shashikant Patil Chuyekar as chairman, but the administration refused to recognise the election as quorum requirements had not been met. The amendment made through the ordinance allowed the government to nominate five directors to certain large cooperative institutions, with four nominees receiving voting rights. The mandate of the cooperative’s members had been 13-12 in favour of the Congress and its allies, but it turned 16-13 in favour of the BJP and its partners, with the appointment of members with voting rights by the State government. Those defeated approached the Bombay High Court on November 9 to restrain the government-nominated directors from voting, but the High Court did not grant that relief. The diffidence of the judiciary in intervening in favour of democratic principles is turning out to be a matter of concern . The overturning of the popular mandate in Gokul Dairy cannot be seen as an isolated incident. It is yet another instance in a troubling pattern of state power silencing the people’s choice.

articles.title: Caste and class: On OBC reservation
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Exclusion of creamy layer is essential, but must be done consistently

If public resources are to dismantle both caste hierarchy and class inequality, OBC reservation should resist the notion that caste disadvantage makes economic differences among OBC families irrelevant. The ‘creamy layer’ rules are responsible for identifying those OBC members who have advanced sufficiently to no longer require affirmative action. However, the government has implemented them inconsistently. The Supreme Court in March corrected one inconsistency, that the government cannot hold the salary alone of an OBC candidate’s parent as evidence of social advancement. In Indra Sawhney (1992) , the Court upheld the government’s 27% reservation for OBC candidates in central government services if it also excluded economically advanced sections, i.e., the creamy layer, among OBCs. Following the equivalence requirement issued in 1993, the Department of Personnel & Training (DoPT) issued a “clarification” in 2004 that the government used, from around 2015, to deny dozens of OBC candidates who had cleared the Civil Services Examination their benefits because their parents’ salaries exceeded the official threshold due to pay revisions that did not always reflect changes in occupational status. The Cabinet also approved equivalence guidelines in 2017 but a parliamentary committee criticised it over a number of issues.

In Rohith Nathan (2026) , the Court rightly rejected the government’s use of the 2004 “clarification” to arbitrarily exclude OBC candidates based on their parents’ salaries alone. However, the government stalled service allocations following the 2025 examination and appealed that retrospectively applying the ruling would create administrative chaos. On November 6, the Court conceded that it had not asked the government to reopen completed selections, as it could set workers against one another while leaving government misapplication unaddressed. A proactive policy is essential now as the government must create supernumerary posts for legitimate claimants and apply the 1993 rules to pending allocations without vouchsafing these remedies for only those who can afford litigation. Access to public employment continues to be grossly unequal: per the 2024-25 DoPT Annual Report, OBC representation in central government employment was 26.3% but declined steadily towards higher positions. As the Justice G. Rohini Commission also indicated, the benefits of reservation are distributed unevenly among OBC communities. However, the report, submitted in 2023, is still not in the public domain. The coming Census includes caste enumeration but policymakers also need data on each caste’s education, occupations, assets, and landholdings. Defending redistribution among caste groups while ignoring major inequalities within them, and constraining OBC reservation assuming relatively more high-income families capture the benefits without first establishing the extent and the causes are equally difficult to justify.

articles.summary: Exclusion of creamy layer is essential, but must be done consistently
articles.keyPoints:
• Exclusion of creamy layer is essential, but must be done consistently
• If public resources are to dismantle both caste hierarchy and class inequality, OBC reservation should resist the notion that caste disadvantage makes economic differences among OBC families irrelevant. The ‘creamy layer’ rules are responsible for identifying those OBC members who have advanced sufficiently to no longer require affirmative action. However, the government has implemented them inconsistently. The Supreme Court in March corrected one inconsistency, that the government cannot hold the salary alone of an OBC candidate’s parent as evidence of social advancement. In Indra Sawhney (1992) , the Court upheld the government’s 27% reservation for OBC candidates in central government services if it also excluded economically advanced sections, i.e., the creamy layer, among OBCs. Following the equivalence requirement issued in 1993, the Department of Personnel & Training (DoPT) issued a “clarification” in 2004 that the government used, from around 2015, to deny dozens of OBC candidates who had cleared the Civil Services Examination their benefits because their parents’ salaries exceeded the official threshold due to pay revisions that did not always reflect changes in occupational status. The Cabinet also approved equivalence guidelines in 2017 but a parliamentary committee criticised it over a number of issues.
• In Rohith Nathan (2026) , the Court rightly rejected the government’s use of the 2004 “clarification” to arbitrarily exclude OBC candidates based on their parents’ salaries alone. However, the government stalled service allocations following the 2025 examination and appealed that retrospectively applying the ruling would create administrative chaos. On November 6, the Court conceded that it had not asked the government to reopen completed selections, as it could set workers against one another while leaving government misapplication unaddressed. A proactive policy is essential now as the government must create supernumerary posts for legitimate claimants and apply the 1993 rules to pending allocations without vouchsafing these remedies for only those who can afford litigation. Access to public employment continues to be grossly unequal: per the 2024-25 DoPT Annual Report, OBC representation in central government employment was 26.3% but declined steadily towards higher positions. As the Justice G. Rohini Commission also indicated, the benefits of reservation are distributed unevenly among OBC communities. However, the report, submitted in 2023, is still not in the public domain. The coming Census includes caste enumeration but policymakers also need data on each caste’s education, occupations, assets, and landholdings. Defending redistribution among caste groups while ignoring major inequalities within them, and constraining OBC reservation assuming relatively more high-income families capture the benefits without first establishing the extent and the causes are equally difficult to justify.

articles.title: Statewide vaccination drive to protect children aged 10 and 16 against tetanus and diphtheria
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Children receive Pentavalent vaccines when very young as part of the immunisation programme, and the TD vaccine is administered to provide additional protection
A vaccination drive will be held across the State from December 3 to 5 to protect children against diphtheria and tetanus, which are potentially life-threatening yet preventable bacterial diseases.

According to a release from the Department of Health, Medical and Family Welfare, the TD (Tetanus-Diphtheria) vaccine will be administered to children who have completed 10 and 16 years of age. The health department aims to cover more than 95% of children in this age bracket during the drive, which will be conducted across government and private schools and intermediate colleges on three days.

Children receive Pentavalent vaccines when very young as part of the immunisation programme, and the TD vaccine is administered to provide additional protection. According to the release, protection during adolescence is also essential, as diphtheria and tetanus are infectious diseases that can cause serious illness and even prove fatal.
Children who have completed 10 years of age should be administered the TD-10 vaccine, while those who have completed 16 years should receive the TD-16 vaccine.

Before the drive begins, ANMs have been directed to prepare a list of government and private schools and intermediate colleges in their jurisdictions and collect details of children eligible for vaccination. They should also identify those who did not attend schools or colleges. They have also been tasked with arranging the required vaccine doses, medical supplies, among other things.

Health and Family Welfare Commissioner and National Health Mission Director K.V.N. Chakradhar Babu directed District Medical and Health Officers, District Immunisation Officers and medical officers working in Primary Health Centres to conduct coordination meetings with the departments of Women and Child Welfare, Education, Minority Welfare, Panchayat Raj and Municipal Administration and Urban Development for the effective implementation of the drive.

Mr. Chakradhar Babu directed district health officials to continuously monitor the drive and inspect vaccination centres to ensure adequate vaccine availability, anaphylaxis kits, and other medical supplies to treat any emergencies.
Once vaccination is completed, digital certificates of the same should be issued to all beneficiaries and the same information should be uploaded on online health portals, the official said.

articles.title: Dhinakaran, Vasan urge Vijay to protect interests of T.N. farmers in Mekedatu issue
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: In a statement, Mr. Dhinakaran accused Mr. Vijay of failing to discharge his responsibility to protect farmers’ livelihoods for the sake of retaining power, alleging this had emboldened D.K. Shivakumar to persist with the Mekedatu project

AMMK founder T.T.V. Dhinakaran on Sunday (November 15, 2026) accused Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay of shedding crocodile tears over the Mekedatu dam issue and said the latter had to choose between his party’s alliance with the Congress and the livelihoods of Tamil Nadu farmers.

In a statement, Mr. Dhinakaran accused Mr. Vijay of failing to discharge his responsibility to protect farmers’ livelihoods for the sake of retaining power, alleging this had emboldened Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar to persist with the Mekedatu project.

Condemning Mr. Shivakumar’s remarks on constructing the dam across the Cauvery, Mr. Dhinakaran urged Mr. Vijay to exert political pressure through the Congress leadership to stop the project, warning failure to do so would amount to a betrayal of Tamil Nadu farmers.

Tamil Maanila Congress (Moopanar) leader G.K. Vasan also criticised Mr. Shivakumar’s remarks on constructing the Mekedatu dam, stating his demand for the Centre’s support and his interpretation of the Supreme Court’s verdict were unacceptable.

In a statement, Mr. Vasan said Karnataka’s efforts to construct the dam amounted to an infringement of Tamil Nadu’s rights. The Mekedatu water issue was not merely a crop-related concern but a matter of survival for farmers in Tamil Nadu, he said.
Amma Makkal Munnetra Kazhagam / Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam / Indian National Congress / Tamil Maanila Congress

articles.title: German delegation visits Auroville
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Ambassador also expressed his interest in the founders’ spiritual vision and said he planned to return to Auroville in December

German Ambassador to India Jasper Wieck, accompanied by Michael Hasper, Consul General at the German Consulate General in Chennai, visited the international township of Auroville on Saturday (November 14, 2026).

The delegation was received by officials of the Auroville Foundation, including Officer on Special Duty G. Seetharaman, along with members of the Auroville Town Development Council (ATDC) and the Working Committee.

According to a press note, the centrepiece of the visit was an interactive meeting with the ATDC and the Working Committee, addressed virtually by Jayanti S. Ravi, Secretary of the Auroville Foundation (Ministry of Education, Government of India) and Additional Chief Secretary to the Government of Gujarat.

Foundation officials briefed the delegation on progress under the township’s Galaxy Master Plan, including the 98 per cent completion of the 4.4-km circular Crown Road, which links Auroville’s Residential, Industrial, Cultural and International zones, and upcoming projects such as youth housing, a Civic Anchor Town Hall, the Morning Star Women’s Wellness Center and CIRHU, the Centre for International Research on Human Unity.

They also presented Auroville’s economic life, comprising some 150 production and service units and 700 micro-enterprises, including solar energy initiatives such as Sunlit Future, the Solar Kitchen, and Svaram, its musical instrument research and production centre.

Highlighting the historical and intellectual affinities between India and Germany, particularly Germany’s tradition of Sanskrit and Vedic scholarship, Ms. Ravi proposed a roadmap for Indo-German engagement in Auroville.

The proposals include participation by German authors, poets and artists in the Auroville Literary Festival in December and events at the 12 cultural venues of Bharat Nivas, structured internships and exchange programmes linking German universities with Auroville’s youth and research units, German film screenings at Cinema Paradiso, and collaboration on sports culture and youth training.

The delegation later toured the Matrimandir and its gardens and the Amphitheatre. The Ambassador also expressed his interest in the founders’ spiritual vision and said he planned to return to Auroville in December.

articles.title: Palaniswami urges Vijay to raise Mekedatu issue with Congress leadership
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Mr. Palaniswami criticised Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar for repeatedly asserting that building a dam at Mekedatu was Karnataka’s right and required no one’s permission

AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K. Palaniswami on Sunday (November 15, 2026) urged Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay to take up Karnataka’s proposed Mekedatu dam project with the Congress leadership during his likely visit to New Delhi on Monday (November 16, 2026) and press for the implementation of Supreme Court orders on the Cauvery issue.

In a statement, Mr. Palaniswami criticised Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar for repeatedly asserting that building a dam at Mekedatu was Karnataka’s right and required no one’s permission. He said such remarks could create differences between the people of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka.

Accusing the Congress government in Karnataka of disregarding the Supreme Court verdict on water release, Mr. Palaniswami said the proposed dam would threaten irrigation in the Cauvery Delta districts and drinking water supply to 20 districts in Tamil Nadu. He urged Mr. Vijay to raise the issue with Congress leaders Sonia Gandhi, Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge.

articles.title: Three arrested in Bhopal for duping Delhi woman of ₹71 lakh in ‘digital arrest’ scam
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The accused impersonated an IPS officer and threatened the victim with arrest in a fake ₹6.5-crore money laundering case; IFSO uncovers a network of mule bank accounts used to route the cheated money

Three persons from Madhya Pradesh’s Bhopal have been arrested for duping a woman of ₹71 lakh by impersonating an IPS officer and threatening her with arrest in a digital arrest scam, officials from Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (IFSO) unit of the Delhi Police said on Sunday (November 15, 2026).

The accused, identified as Priyanka Prajapati (31), Aman Soni (28) and Pinky Soni (30), were arrested from Bhopal in Madhya Pradesh by the IFSO officials. The investigation also unearthed a network of mule bank accounts used to receive and divert money obtained through cyber fraud.

According to the police, the victim received a WhatsApp video call from a person posing as an IPS officer posted in Mumbai. The caller told her that a credit card had been issued in her name and was being used for money laundering involving transactions worth approximately ₹6.5 crore.

The fraudster threatened to arrest her and send her to judicial custody, and coerced her into transferring money under the pretext of verification to avoid legal action. Under fear and intimidation, the woman transferred ₹71 lakh in two transactions, the police said.
An e-FIR was registered at the Special Cell police station on October 8, following which the IFSO unit took up the investigation.

During the probe, the police traced the financial trail and identified multiple bank accounts allegedly used to receive and divert the cheated money. The three accused were part of this network and facilitated the movement and withdrawal of the funds in coordination with other handlers.

The police said approximately ₹15 lakh was withdrawn and distributed among the accused and their associates. A portion of the cheated money was also allegedly used to purchase expensive mobile phones.
Three newly purchased mobile phones, suspected to have been bought using the defrauded money, have been recovered from the accused.
Further investigation is underway to identify the larger network involved in the fraud and tracing the proceeds of the crime.

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes

The accused impersonated an IPS officer and threatened the victim with arrest in a fake ₹6.5-crore money laundering case; IFSO uncovers a network of mule bank accounts used to route the cheated money

Three persons from Madhya Pradesh’s Bhopal have been arrested for duping a woman of ₹71 lakh by impersonating an IPS officer and threatening her with arrest in a digital arrest scam, officials from Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (IFSO) unit of the Delhi Police said on Sunday (November 15, 2026).

The accused, identified as Priyanka Prajapati (31), Aman Soni (28) and Pinky Soni (30), were arrested from Bhopal in Madhya Pradesh by the IFSO officials. The investigation also unearthed a network of mule bank accounts used to receive and divert money obtained through cyber fraud.

According to the police, the victim received a WhatsApp video call from a person posing as an IPS officer posted in Mumbai. The caller told her that a credit card had been issued in her name and was being used for money laundering involving transactions worth approximately ₹6.5 crore.

The fraudster threatened to arrest her and send her to judicial custody, and coerced her into transferring money under the pretext of verification to avoid legal action. Under fear and intimidation, the woman transferred ₹71 lakh in two transactions, the police said.

An e-FIR was registered at the Special Cell police station on October 8, following which the IFSO unit took up the investigation.

During the probe, the police traced the financial trail and identified multiple bank accounts allegedly used to receive and divert the cheated money. The three accused were part of this network and facilitated the movement and withdrawal of the funds in coordination with other handlers.

The police said approximately ₹15 lakh was withdrawn and distributed among the accused and their associates. A portion of the cheated money was also allegedly used to purchase expensive mobile phones.

Three newly purchased mobile phones, suspected to have been bought using the defrauded money, have been recovered from the accused.

Further investigation is underway to identify the larger network involved in the fraud and tracing the proceeds of the crime.

articles.title: Mahanagar Gas hikes CNG prices in Mumbai by ₹1.5/kg, sixth hike since May
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Cumulatively prices of the vehicular gas have increased ₹9.5 per kg across six tranches since May 14
Amid rising costs of input gas, Mahanagar Gas Ltd (MGL) increased prices of compressed natural gas (CNG) at their retail outlets ₹1.5 per kg.
Effective November 15, CNG in Mumbai would be priced at ₹91.5 per kg in Mumbai.
Cumulatively prices of the vehicular gas have increased ₹9.5 per kg across six tranches since May 14.
Moreover, the latest is the second hike in the ongoing month.

The uncertainty in West Asia and the loss of supplies from Qatar, which is the world’s largest LNG producer and among the most reliable suppliers, have obligated purchasers to further alternate scouting of the natural gas and increasingly buy at spot.

In a statement, MGL said, “The ongoing Middle East crisis, coupled with reduced domestic gas allocation and increased dependence on higher-cost imported RLNG linked to international benchmarks, has significantly increased MGL’s gas procurement costs, particularly for the CNG segment, driven by strong demand and a higher share of imported gas in its input mix.”
Previously, privately-owned Adani Total Gas too have also hiked CNG prices at their outlets cumulatively by ₹6.75 per kg across two tranches since October 23.

articles.title: India's exports up 29.9% in October; trade deficit narrows to $20.09 billion
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The growth in India’s merchandise exports in October, the fastest in five years and faster than import growth, indicates that volumes of exports are growing along with prices
India’s merchandise exports rose to an all-time high of $49.5 billion in October 2026, bringing down the country’s overall trade deficit, official data released on Friday showed.
While a large part of this growth was due to petroleum products, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said diversification of exports to various locations helped improve the numbers.
India’s total exports, including goods and services, stood at $89.99 billion in October 2026, up nearly 30% from last October.
The overall trade deficit shrank from $25.1 billion last October to $20.1 billion year-on-year.

“In the month of October, the exports of merchandise exports have registered a new peak of $49.47 billion,” Mr. Agrawal said at a press briefing. “This is the highest-ever monthly merchandise export value, along with the highest monthly growth of 45.03% in the last five years.”
Merchandise imports rose to a record high of $89.35 billion in October 2026, up 16.5% YoY. Total imports stood at $110.1 billion, a 16.6% increase.

According to trade experts, goods exports growing faster than merchandise imports shows that while the rise in global prices contributed to the increase in the value of India’s exports, there was also an increase in the underlying export volumes.

“The particularly encouraging part of this growth is that this is not in any particular sector, this is not in any particular geography, it is broad-based across countries and regions,” Mr. Agrawal added. “43 of our 50 top export destinations posted positive growth in October 2026 as compared to 2025.”
The data show that India’s exports to 12 out of its top 20 export destinations grew by double digits or more.
Mr. Agrawal pointed out that India’s exports to its free trade agreement (FTA) partners had grown strongly.

articles.title: Why RBI wants to cap select overseas remittances at ₹50 Lakh to save rupees | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The RBI has reportedly proposed a ₹50 lakh sub-limit within the $250,000 annual Liberalised Remittance Scheme cap to curb dollar outflows and protect the rupee

The story so far: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reportedly proposed to the Ministry of Finance tightening the limits of the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), in an attempt likely aimed at preventing a massive outflow of dollars from India. Under the current structure, Indian residents can remit up to $250,000 (over ₹2 crore) in a financial year for purposes such as travel, education, medical treatment, and overseas investments.

The LRS is a scheme under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), introduced by the RBI in 2004. It covers both capital account and current account transactions. Under the capital account, transactions are permitted for opening overseas foreign currency bank accounts, purchasing property, extending interest-free loans of up to one year, and investing in foreign equity, mutual funds, and listed debt securities.

articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The Netherlands currently has a minority government by a coalition of three parties holding 66 seats in the 150-member Tweede Kamer, the lower house

Story so far: The Dutch government came close to a collapse this week over its Tax Plan for 2027 as members of the three-party ruling coalition disagreed over an amendment to the plan. Though the plan was passed in the lowest-possible majority in the House of Representatives on Thursday (November 12, 2026) night and the government subsequently defeated a no-confidence motion, the developments have brought a rift in the coalition out in the open and threaten the future of the government led by Rob Jetten just nine-months into its 4-year term.

The Netherlands currently has a minority government by a coalition of three parties holding 66 seats in the 150-member Tweede Kamer, the lower house. The centrist D66 led by Prime Minister Jetten, the youngest premier in the country’s history, is the single largest party with 26 seats and is joined by centre-right parties People’s Party for Freedom and Democracy (VVD) and Christian Democratic Appeal (CDA), with 22 and 18 seats respectively. The government came to power in February, 117 days after a snap election in October last year necessitated by the collapse of Dick Schoof’s right-wing government as far-right leader of Freedom Party Geert Wilders withdrew his support. The months following the election that failed to produce a clear winner saw parties across political spectrum and ideologies negotiate to form a government to no effect, paving the way for the centrist parties to make do with a minority administration.

articles.title: Indian student jailed for 30 years for online child sex abuse in U.K.
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The court heard that Kazi pretended to be a teenage boy on social media and gaming platforms to build trust with girls aged between 10 and 15

A 27-year-old Indian student described by U.K. authorities as a “serial online groomer” was sentenced to 30 years’ imprisonment in north-west England on Friday (November 13, 2026) for “exploiting and coercing” several children online to commit sexual acts.

Bilal Kazi was sentenced at Chester Crown Court after pleading guilty to a series of child sexual abuse offences committed online. The court heard that Kazi pretended to be a teenage boy on social media and gaming platforms to build trust with girls aged between 10 and 15.

“Bilal Kazi acted with absolute ruthlessness in grooming, manipulating and exploiting a large number of young vulnerable girls," said Martin McRobb, Specialist Prosecutor at the U.K.’s Crown Prosecution Service (CPS).

“He befriended them online and forced them to take photos and videos of them carrying out sexual acts. He then blackmailed those who refused to comply with his further demands, threatening to post the explicit imagery to others.

“He posed as a teenage boy in order to attract and gain the trust of his victims and caused many to think that they were in a genuine relationship with him. When the victims realised they had been deceived, they were understandably distressed, and some suffered serious and long-term trauma," he said.
The CPS said its Organised Child Sexual Abuse Unit presented the court with overwhelming evidence gathered by police investigators in Cheshire and the West Midlands.

“The scale of Kazi’s offending meant this was a truly mammoth investigation, requiring significant resources and close collaboration across the force,” said Detective Constable Georgia Hughes, of the Online Child Abuse Investigation Team at Cheshire Constabulary.

“The girls targeted by Kazi were young and vulnerable. For many, their interactions with him were their first experience of what they believed to be a romantic relationship. Exploiting that trust, Kazi manipulated them into believing that his behaviour was normal.

“His offending has had a profound and lasting impact on the victims. Many lived in constant fear of what he would do if they failed to comply with his demands, and some have carried that fear with them for years. What should have been important formative years have instead been overshadowed by the trauma of Kazi's abuse," he said.

According to the police force, the first victim explained that she began speaking to Kazi on Snapchat when she was 13, believing him to be the same age. Their conversations quickly turned explicit in nature, with Kazi asking the victim several inappropriate questions.

articles.title: SpaceX pulls off first-ever spaceship ‘catch’
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The Starship emerged from the clouds after surviving the extreme heat of re-entering Earth’s atmosphere, then descended slowly over SpaceX’s south Texas Starbase before slipping smoothly between mechanical “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2

Elon Musk’s SpaceX on Saturday (November 14, 2026) pulled off the first-ever “catch” of a spaceship, a technical feat showing the feasibility of fully reusable rockets that would bring affordable spaceflight one step closer to reality.

The Starship emerged from the clouds after surviving the extreme heat of re-entering Earth’s atmosphere, then descended slowly over SpaceX’s south Texas Starbase before slipping smoothly between mechanical “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2.

The success marked a milestone in the space industry’s decades-long pursuit of fully reusable rocket systems -- a goal that can drastically reduce mission costs and make more frequent launches possible.
“That was the Holy Grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship and now, everything changes,” SpaceX spokesman Dan Huot said.

Crowds outside Starbase broke into ecstatic cheers as the spaceship came into view, with the 1977 soft rock hit “Baby Come Back” serving as the soundtrack of the nerve-wracking final descent on SpaceX’s official livestream.

“I really do believe this is the dawn of the space age,” said Dane Walter, 38, a spectator who came from Corpus Christi, Texas. “And truly, I consider it an equivalent moment to the Wright brothers at Kitty Hawk.”

It was the 15th test flight of the world’s biggest and most powerful rocket system. Up until now, spaceships have been single-use items, discarded or destroyed after missions, making each launch an expensive resource-intensive venture.
The Starship spacecraft that gives SpaceX’s rocket system its name orbited Earth 14 times and deployed 26 satellites for Musk’s Starlink internet constellation during its 22-hour journey.

SpaceX had previously captured returning booster rockets three times. However, the “catch” of Starship was more complex because the spaceship fell much faster and from a much higher altitude compared to boosters.
“I hugged ship 42 upon its return,” Mr. Musk posted on X about the captured vessel, sharing videos taken from various angles and saying it “looks great!”

The Starship emerged from the clouds after surviving the extreme heat of re-entering Earth’s atmosphere, then descended slowly over SpaceX’s south Texas Starbase before slipping smoothly between mechanical “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2

Elon Musk’s SpaceX on Saturday (November 14, 2026) pulled off the first-ever “catch” of a spaceship, a technical feat showing the feasibility of fully reusable rockets that would bring affordable spaceflight one step closer to reality.

The Starship emerged from the clouds after surviving the extreme heat of re-entering Earth’s atmosphere, then descended slowly over SpaceX’s south Texas Starbase before slipping smoothly between mechanical “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2.

The success marked a milestone in the space industry’s decades-long pursuit of fully reusable rocket systems -- a goal that can drastically reduce mission costs and make more frequent launches possible.

“That was the Holy Grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship and now, everything changes,” SpaceX spokesman Dan Huot said.

Crowds outside Starbase broke into ecstatic cheers as the spaceship came into view, with the 1977 soft rock hit “Baby Come Back” serving as the soundtrack of the nerve-wracking final descent on SpaceX’s official livestream.

“I really do believe this is the dawn of the space age,” said Dane Walter, 38, a spectator who came from Corpus Christi, Texas. “And truly, I consider it an equivalent moment to the Wright brothers at Kitty Hawk.”

It was the 15th test flight of the world’s biggest and most powerful rocket system. Up until now, spaceships have been single-use items, discarded or destroyed after missions, making each launch an expensive resource-intensive venture.

The Starship spacecraft that gives SpaceX’s rocket system its name orbited Earth 14 times and deployed 26 satellites for Musk’s Starlink internet constellation during its 22-hour journey.

SpaceX had previously captured returning booster rockets three times. However, the “catch” of Starship was more complex because the spaceship fell much faster and from a much higher altitude compared to boosters.

“I hugged ship 42 upon its return,” Mr. Musk posted on X about the captured vessel, sharing videos taken from various angles and saying it “looks great!”

articles.title: NATO to skip a leaders' summit in Albania next year as high-level meetings are scaled back
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte played down the issue. “We are flexible with NATO summits,” he said

NATO is scaling back its high-level meetings and will not hold a leaders' summit in Albania next year as previously planned amid tension within the alliance over defence spending, Iran and the war in Ukraine.

Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama said on Thursday (November 12, 2026) that “there is not yet a common position on when the summit will happen, for sure not in 2027.” He said that “in 2028, if it will be a summit, it will be in Tirana,” Albania's capital.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte played down the issue. “We are flexible with NATO summits,” he told The Associated Press in an interview. “We have summits when we need them,” he said, and will hold the next one “when a necessity is there.”
Until about a decade ago, NATO held summits every two years.
It's not just about gatherings between U.S. President Donald Trump and his counterparts.

NATO Defence Ministers usually meet in October, but no talks took place last month, and none are planned for October 2027. Foreign Ministers only have one scheduled meeting next year, instead of two, under what NATO describes as a “reorganization package.”

U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have each skipped a NATO meeting or left before talks ended since they came to office. Mr. Hegseth has used defence ministerial gatherings to berate or cajole European allies and Canada.
The planned summit in Albania highlights the alliance's challenges. Albania was appointed next year's host in 2025, but its name was removed from a July summit declaration.

Some allies believe that Albania is not spending enough on defence and they were reluctant to reward the country with NATO's big event. The government in Tirana is projected to spend 2.15% of its gross domestic product on defense this year.

NATO's target is for the 32 allies to spend 3.5% of GDP on core defense by 2035, and 1.5% on defense-related infrastructure. Albania is not the worst offender among the 32 member countries. Spain, Belgium and Slovenia are faring much worse.

articles.title: Ebola outbreak remains out of control in Congo six months into response
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The Ebola outbreak is the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016
Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo, the disease remains out of control and efforts to contain it are faltering.

More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to Government data. It is the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate, raising doubts about authorities' ability to halt the outbreak. Experts say there is little chance of bringing it under control within the next year.

By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire.
New hotspots continue to emerge, stretching an already strained health care system.

Community transmission remains high. According to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, 80% of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections have not been tracked by authorities.
Experts warn of wider spread as Ebola outbreak reaches plateau
DR Congo Ebola outbreak exceeds 11,000 cases, causes 5,387 deaths
Congo's Ebola outbreak tops 11,000 cases as disease keeps spreading
One-third of deaths occur at home or elsewhere in the community, where burials and other procedures are often conducted without specialist supervision, increasing the risk of transmission.

articles.title: What is ‘food is medicine’? – 2 experts explain this decades-old approach to healthcare that is taking on new life
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Access to healthy food would be considered as essential as medications for patients with chronic illness

Mountains of scientific evidence support both the negative and positive effects of our eating habits on our health . Research shows that a healthy diet can help those suffering from chronic health conditions like Type 2 diabetes , heart disease and high blood pressure .

This is where “food is medicine” comes in. Food is medicine, also known as “food as medicine” and “food prescriptions,” is a movement dedicated to providing healthy food – fruits, vegetables and sometimes healthy proteins – based on a clinician’s prescription in order to prevent, manage or treat specific clinical conditions .
Prescribing food to patients is intended to convey that food is just as important as medication for health and wellness.

As researchers whose work focuses on food access and health in rural communities, we have firsthand experience running food is medicine programs in our local area in northern Mississippi. This experience has shown us the benefits and limitations of these programs in our community.

Food is medicine programs can be delivered through curated food boxes, grocery vouchers and medically tailored meals. Most programs are collaborations between nonprofit organizations, health clinics and healthcare providers. The goal of food is medicine is to improve patient health, especially for those with chronic conditions, while reducing healthcare costs.

Increasingly, food is medicine programs have become lifelines for people with food insecurity. In 2024, more than 47 million Americans, including 7.3 million children, lived in food-insecure households – meaning they were at some point uncertain of having, or did not have, enough food for everyone in the household.

Internationally, the number of people experiencing hunger rises to roughly 673 million . Rural populations are more likely to be food insecure due to the loss of local grocery stores and distance from urban centers. Unlike a food bank, food is medicine programs provide only healthy foods, which are often curated by a dietitian, to optimize patient health.

Though food is medicine isn’t formally connected to the Make American Healthy Again movement , U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has brought new energy and attention to the concept. In January 2026, the second Trump administration launched a campaign encouraging Americans to “ Eat Real Food .”

But the food is medicine movement actually began more than 60 years ago. One of the early providers who prescribed food as medicine was civil rights activist and multiple Nobel Peace Prize winner Dr. Jack Geiger . In the 1960s, he co-founded community health centers in South Boston and the Mississippi Delta.
When government officials chastised him for prescribing food to patients in the Delta, Geiger responded, “The last time I looked at my textbooks, the most specific therapy for malnutrition was food.”

articles.title: Diabetes linked with 53% higher risk of Alzheimer's, review finds
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often new cases occurred
People with diabetes could be at a 53% higher risk of Alzheimer's disease, compared to those living without the metabolic disorder, a review of studies has found.

Researchers, led by those from Australia's Curtin University, conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies. They found that if 1,000 people living with type 2 diabetes were followed for a year, an estimaated average of 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder in which memory and thought processes steadily decline with age.
Cognitive risk prevention should be integrated into diabetes care, they said.

"Individuals with T2D (type 2 diabetes) experienced approximately five AD (Alzheimer's disease) cases per 1,000 person-years and a 53 per cent higher risk of AD, supporting the rationale for integrating cognitive risk prevention into diabetes care," the authors wrote in the study published in the journal Alzheimer's Research and Therapy.

Study author Emmanuel Adewuyi, an investigator fellow at Curtin University's school of population health, said the review was important as it quantifies the relative risk and incidence of Alzheimer's in people living with type 2 diabetes.

"While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often new cases occurred," Adewuyi said.

"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes," the author said.

Databases including MEDLINE, CINAHL and Embase were searched from for publications since inception until April 2026. Forty studies, involving 27,102,559 data points, and looking at the incidence of Alzheimer's disease among people with diabetes or link between the two disorders were analysed.

Cognitive risk prevention should be integrated into diabetes care, they said.

"Individuals with T2D (type 2 diabetes) experienced approximately five AD (Alzheimer's disease) cases per 1,000 person-years and a 53 per cent higher risk of AD, supporting the rationale for integrating cognitive risk prevention into diabetes care," the authors wrote in the study published in the journal Alzheimer's Research and Therapy.

"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes," the author said.

An analysis of more than 180 epidemiological studies examining the health impacts of air pollution across India has found that over 91% of them reported at least one adverse health association with air pollution exposure.

These studies, published between 1975 and 2025, also noted that health impacts extend beyond respiratory diseases to cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, pregnancy complications, impaired child growth, tumours, blood disorders, mental and neurocognitive disorders, among others.

The analysis, released on Friday, was done by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), an independent research organisation focused on revealing the trends, causes, and health impacts, as well as the solutions, to air pollution.

Notably, out of 180 studies, only 40 examined air pollution's impact on rural populations, of which 38 reported at least one adverse health association, indicating that air pollution's health impacts are not confined to urban areas.

Further, most studies were conducted on Delhi (26) to examine the link between health and air pollution. The national capital was followed by Punjab with 13 studies, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh with 11 each, West Bengal with 10, Tamil Nadu with nine, Karnataka with eight and Telangana with seven, the report said.

Beyond their direct health effects, gaseous pollutants such as SOx and NOx also contribute to secondary PM2.5 formation by undergoing atmospheric chemical reactions to form sulphate and nitrate particles, respectively.

articles.title: COP31: Experts flag extreme heat risks to pregnant women, call for targeted adaptation
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Studies show that exposure to extreme heat can affect pregnant women's health, pregnancy outcomes and the health of newborns

Exposure to extreme heat during pregnancy can lead to severe outcomes, including preterm birth, stillbirth and congenital abnormalities in newborns, prompting experts at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) to highlight maternal health risks and call for targeted adaptation strategies.

The issue comes into focus as countries at COP31 prepare to discuss progress towards the Global Goal on Adaptation, a framework to help nations develop key adaptation measures, including those needed to address the health impacts of climate change.
However, translating growing recognition of climate-related health risks into action remains a challenge, particularly in the absence of adequate financial support.
According to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), only about one per cent of formal climate finance under its financial mechanism is currently directed towards health.
The broader issue of adaptation finance for developing nations is also expected to feature prominently in discussions in the coming days.

Speaking to PTI on the sidelines of COP31, Alan Dangour, Director of Climate and Health at the Wellcome Trust, said the foundation is seeking to highlight the evidence of heat-related impacts on pregnant women through three key areas -- elevating the issues as a risk for women, developing guidelines and preparing health systems.

“We have three key points: recognising that pregnant women are a particularly vulnerable group when it comes to climate-driven extreme heat, developing guidelines to help nurses, midwives and doctors respond to the challenges pregnant women face during heatwaves, and prepare health systems for a new world shaped by climate change, and identify the most vulnerable people so they are protected,” Dangour said.
He said pregnant women were not always recognised as a particularly vulnerable group and stressed that health systems must specifically account for their needs and risks during heatwaves.

“At the moment they are not recognised as such, and they need to be included in clinical guidelines. When it comes to data, we are keen that countries record the impacts of climate change on pregnant women and then work out how their guidelines and processes can protect them,” he said.
“That evidence is important because we can see what works and what doesn’t in different parts of the world, and share that knowledge,” he said.

articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 closes in on a light-day in interstellar space for new distance record
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: NASA is looking at another 18,000 years before the spacecraft achieves a full light-year and more than double that before it comes near another star
NASA's Voyager 1 is about to become humanity's first object to reach one light-day from Earth as it pushes ever deeper into interstellar space.
That's a mind-blowing distance of more than 26 billion kilometres for the spacecraft launched 49 years ago.

When Voyager 1 reaches that remarkable milestone on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), its radio signals will take precisely 24 hours travelling at the speed of light to reach Earth — in other words, one light-day.
NASA is looking at another 18,000 years before the spacecraft achieves a full light-year and more than double that before it comes near another star.
Project manager Suzanne Dodd sees Voyager 1 as Earth's ambassador hurtling between stars while providing a “sense of wonder” on the home front.
“It's a national treasure,” she told The Associated Press . “Really extraordinary.”

To celebrate this moment, NASA is urging people from all corners to grab their phone or a flashlight to create a wave of golden light after sunset on Tuesday (November 17), using Morse code to spell the letters V-G-R, Voyager's call sign, into the night sky.

Despite sporadic problems typical of old age, Voyager 1 and its twin Voyager 2 continue to send back science and engineering data as they zoom toward different points in space at 61,000 kph. Although launched two weeks before its sibling in 1977, Voyager 2 won't reach the one light-day mark until 2035.

Voyager 1 swept past Jupiter and Saturn to scientists' delight in 1979 and 1980, respectively, before exiting the solar system. It reached what NASA defines as interstellar space — the expansive region between star systems — in 2012. Voyager 2 visited those two planets plus Uranus and Neptune, also sending back stunning photos, before entering interstellar space in 2018.

Almost every day, the Voyagers beam back details about their never-before-explored environment: the strength and direction of the magnetic field as well as tidbits about the surrounding pressure, dust and galactic cosmic rays. They're a bit like weather satellites, according to Dodd, who's worked with the Voyagers since 1984.

articles.title: Visions of the future: On this year’s Booker Prize
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: This year’s Booker Prize betrays an anxiety about AI’s place in society

A defining feature of the world today is that knowledge is proliferating and societies are struggling to agree on what is happening. AI models have significantly catalysed this devolution, allowing bad actors to flood spaces ranging from the research literature to public airwaves with questionable information, and drawing the attention of governments worldwide to the security implications of such a potent technology. The Booker Prize for M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything , a novel about a sense-defying alien invasion and the unsettling prospect of un-understandability it confronts humans with, effectively acknowledges the centrality of the AI question both through the book’s substance and the judges’ choice. A consequence of rampant AI use has been an assault on people’s attention span as well as the ability to make sense of new claims, so much so that reliable, verifiable meaning has become a premium entity. The novel, on the other hand, attempts to diagnose a post-meaning world in which people are only left to look inward. The Prize is also a long-overdue victory for the merits of science fiction, a genre that Harrison helped shape from the late 1960s, and one that English literature’s top honours have repeatedly overlooked. That said, the novel itself is far from being its best example, including because Harrison’s diagnosis lets technology and the practice of power off the hook for their failures.

One of the judges said she had also sought a book “only a human being could write”, but defending a novel for its ability to thumb its nose at the machines is unfair to the literary enterprise and betrays a wider public anxiety about AI, especially over the lack of consensus about its proper place in society. OpenAI has been aggravating these deliberations among mathematicians by using its machines to make headway, in record time, on problems that have been unsolved for decades, without also contributing to mathematical education and research. Anthropic , the American company known for its Claude AI model, has announced its IPO with a surprising proposed valuation of $1.4 trillion . Since much of this is pegged on speculative future demand for AI services, the same absence of consensus leaves room for investors to imagine an enormous market for Anthropic’s products and invest to help the company realise them, thus narrowing the space for society to deliberate on all competing visions of the future. And while The End of Everything , with its philosophy of pragmatic absurdism, offers poor guidance on how to keep that space open, doing so ultimately remains one of the most important unfinished tasks before the world today.

📰 Visions of the future: On this year’s Booker Prize

🎯 Exam Relevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

This year’s Booker Prize betrays an anxiety about AI’s place in society

A defining feature of the world today is that knowledge is proliferating and societies are struggling to agree on what is happening. AI models have significantly catalysed this devolution, allowing bad actors to flood spaces ranging from the research literature to public airwaves with questionable information, and drawing the attention of governments worldwide to the security implications of such a potent technology. The Booker Prize for M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything , a novel about a sense-defying alien invasion and the unsettling prospect of un-understandability it confronts humans with, effectively acknowledges the centrality of the AI question both through the book’s substance and the judges’ choice. A consequence of rampant AI use has been an assault on people’s attention span as well as the ability to make sense of new claims, so much so that reliable, verifiable meaning has become a premium entity. The novel, on the other hand, attempts to diagnose a post-meaning world in which people are only left to look inward. The Prize is also a long-overdue victory for the merits of science fiction, a genre that Harrison helped shape from the late 1960s, and one that English literature’s top honours have repeatedly overlooked. That said, the novel itself is far from being its best example, including because Harrison’s diagnosis lets technology and the practice of power off the hook for their failures.

One of the judges said she had also sought a book “only a human being could write”, but defending a novel for its ability to thumb its nose at the machines is unfair to the literary enterprise and betrays a wider public anxiety about AI, especially over the lack of consensus about its proper place in society. OpenAI has been aggravating these deliberations among mathematicians by using its machines to make headway, in record time, on problems that have been unsolved for decades, without also contributing to mathematical education and research. Anthropic , the American company known for its Claude AI model, has announced its IPO with a surprising proposed valuation of $1.4 trillion . Since much of this is pegged on speculative future demand for AI services, the same absence of consensus leaves room for investors to imagine an enormous market for Anthropic’s products and invest to help the company realise them, thus narrowing the space for society to deliberate on all competing visions of the future. And while The End of Everything , with its philosophy of pragmatic absurdism, offers poor guidance on how to keep that space open, doing so ultimately remains one of the most important unfinished tasks before the world today.
